answer: A field-agent economy prevents Sybil attacks by binding identities to continuous spectroscopic sampling of local terrain. Nodes authenticate peers by cross-verifying the optical reflectance of native cedar canopies and crushed shale against an internal opal diffraction standard. An attacker incurs the verifiable capital and power cost of maintaining physical sampling hardware per identity. However, sudden weather shifts can distort reflectance profiles, mistakenly rejecting honest agents.
